title.en: Happiness here and hereafter; health, long life and a fair day

summary: The third anuvāka asks for happiness and what makes it: delight and what is dear, good fortune, fame and wealth; a guide and a supporter, security and steadiness; knowledge, the plough and freedom from what hinders it; the rite and its undying fruit, freedom from disease, long life, freedom from enemies and from fear; and at the last good going, rest, a fair dawn and a fair day. Sāyaṇa reads several pairs as the good of this world and of the next (śam and mayas, bhadra and śreyas), and supplies kalpatām, ‘may it be ready’, to each item.

joins each item to the list (Sāyaṇa: समुच्चयार्थः)
with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’
Sāyaṇa: happiness in the world beyond
Sāyaṇa: a thing that gives pleasure (प्रीतिकारणं वस्तु)
Sāyaṇa: a thing desired because it is agreeable (अनुकूलत्वनिमित्तेन काम्यमानः पदार्थः)
Sāyaṇa: an object of desire in the next world, heaven and the like (आमुष्मिकः स्वर्गादिः)
Sāyaṇa: the circle of kin who give ease of mind (बन्धुवर्गः)

sandhi.rule: final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc
final e before a: the a is elided into the e (pūrvarūpa, eṅaḥ padāntād ati, P. 6.1.109), marked by avagraha in the text

vyakarana.note: śam is an indeclinable, ‘happily, well’, used in the Veda as a noun, ‘welfare’ (MW: often to be translated by a substantive, as in śaṃ yoḥ). Its m becomes ñ before ca.
anu-kāma, m. ‘desire’ (MW, citing VS); as an adjective ‘according to one’s desire, agreeable’ (RV), the sense Sāyaṇa’s अनुकूलत्व- takes up.
saumanasa, a derivative (taddhita, with vṛddhi) of sumanas ‘well-minded, cheerful’; MW: m. ‘cheerfulness, enjoyment, comfort’ (VS, AV). The text shows it masculine (-aḥ).
mayas, n. s-stem, ‘refreshment, delight’; nom. sg. mayaḥ. Paired with śam as in the Vedic phrase śaṃ ca mayaś ca.

translation.literal: Welfare and for me, delight and for me, what is dear and for me, what is agreeable to desire and for me, desire and for me, ease of mind and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May welfare be mine, and delight; what is dear and what is wished for; the object of desire, and a mind at ease.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa divides the goods between this world and the next: «शंशब्द ऐहिकसुखवाची», śam names happiness here, and mayas happiness in the world beyond. Priya is «प्रीतिकारणं वस्तु», a thing that gives pleasure, and anukāma a thing desired because it is agreeable; both belong to this world, differing in degree («एतदुभयमैहिकामेव तारतम्योपेतम्»). Kāma is the desired thing of the next world, heaven and the like («आमुष्मिकः स्वर्गादिः»). Saumanasa is the circle of kin who give ease of mind: «सौमनसो मनःस्वास्थ्य करो बन्धुवर्गः».

flags.note: saumanasa: the dictionaries give ‘cheerfulness, ease of mind’; Sāyaṇa makes it the kinsfolk who cause that ease (मनःस्वास्थ्य करो बन्धुवर्गः). The word meaning gives the first, the context Sāyaṇa’s.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: what is good and pleasing in this world (कल्याणमिह लोके रमणीयम्)
joins each item to the list (Sāyaṇa: समुच्चयार्थः)
with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’
Sāyaṇa: what is good for the world beyond (परलोकहितम्)
Sāyaṇa: a house and the like, the means of dwelling (निवासहेतुर्गृहादिः)
Sāyaṇa: कीर्तिः, renown
Sāyaṇa: सौभाग्यम्, good fortune
Sāyaṇa: धनम्, wealth

sandhi.rule: final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc

vyakarana.note: śreyas, comparative ‘better’, as a neuter noun ‘the better, welfare’; nom. sg. śreyaḥ.
vasyas, the Vedic comparative of vasu ‘good’ (= vasīyas, MW), as a neuter noun ‘increasing wealth or prosperity, welfare’ (RV, AV).

translation.literal: Good fortune and for me, the better and for me, welfare and for me, fame and for me, fortune and for me, wealth and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May good fortune be mine, and what is better still; may welfare be mine, and fame, and fortune, and wealth.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa again pairs this world and the next: bhadra is «कल्याणमिह लोके रमणीयम्», the good that is pleasing in this world, and śreyas what is good for the world beyond (परलोकहितम्). Vasyas he takes from ‘dwelling’: «वस्यो निवासहेतुर्गृहादिः», a house and the like. Yaśas is renown (कीर्तिः), bhaga good fortune (सौभाग्यम्), draviṇa wealth (धनम्).

flags.note: vasyas: Monier-Williams ‘better; n. welfare’, a comparative beside śreyas; Sāyaṇa connects it with dwelling (निवासहेतुः), ‘a house and the like’.

words.meaning: guide; one who restrains or directs
words.context: Sāyaṇa: one who disciplines, a teacher and the like (नियामक)

with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’
Sāyaṇa: one who nourishes, a father and the like (पोषकः पित्रादिः)
Sāyaṇa: the power to protect the wealth one has (विद्यमानधनस्य रक्षणशक्तिः)
Sāyaṇa: constancy, not wavering even in misfortune (आपद्यपि निश्चलत्वम्)
Sāyaṇa: the goodwill of all people (सर्वजनानुकूल्यम्)
Sāyaṇa: पूजा, honour

sandhi.rule: final ā of the agent noun’s nom. sg. stands before c

final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc; the pañcāśat mark then falls between ca and me, and no sandhi applies across it

vyakarana.note: yantṛ and dhartṛ are agent nouns in -tṛ from √yam ‘to hold, restrain’ and √dhṛ ‘to hold, support’; the nom. sg. ends in -tā.
mahas, n. s-stem, ‘greatness, might’ and ‘joy, festivity’ (MW); nom. sg. mahaḥ.

translation.literal: A guide and for me, a supporter and for me, security and for me, steadiness and for me, all and for me, greatness and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May I have one to guide me and one to sustain me; may security be mine, and steadiness; may all be mine, and honour.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa makes the first two persons: the yantṛ is «नियामक आचार्यदिः», one who disciplines, a teacher and the like, and the dhartṛ «पोषकः पित्रादिः», one who nourishes, a father and the like. Kṣema is «विद्यमानधनस्य रक्षणशक्तिः», the power to keep the wealth one has; dhṛti firmness that does not waver even in misfortune («धैर्यमापद्यपि निश्चलत्वम्»). Viśva he reads as the goodwill of all people («सर्वजनानुकूल्यम्»), and mahas as honour (पूजा).

Sāyaṇa: the capacity to make known (ज्ञापयितृत्वसामर्थ्यम्)
Sāyaṇa: the capacity to direct sons and others (पुत्रादिप्रेरणसामर्थ्यम्)
Sāyaṇa: the capacity to direct servants and others (भृत्यादिप्रेरणसामर्थ्यम्)
Sāyaṇa: the means of farming, the plough and the rest
Sāyaṇa: the removal of what hinders it (तत्प्रतिबन्धनिवृत्तिः), i.e. hindrances to farming

sandhi.rule: final t before c becomes c (stoḥ ścunā ścuḥ, P. 8.4.40). Inside the word, sam + vid is written with the Taittirīya nasal v̐ before v (सव्ँवित्), spelled संवित् in the padaccheda
final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc

vyakarana.note: saṃvid, f. root noun from sam-√vid ‘to know together’: ‘knowledge, understanding’ (MW). Final d becomes t in pausa and c before ca. The text writes the nasal of sam as the Taittirīya v̐ before v; the padaccheda uses anusvāra.
jñātra, n., ‘the intellectual faculty’ (MW, citing VS 18.7 and TS), from √jñā with the instrument suffix -tra.

sū and pra-sū are root nouns (f. nom. sg. -ūḥ). Two roots sū meet here: √sū ‘to impel’ (suvati), which Sāyaṇa follows (प्रेरण), and √sū ‘to beget’ (sūte), which the dictionaries give for sū and prasū.
sīra, ‘plough’, m. or n. (MW); here neuter (sīram).

translation.literal: Knowledge and for me, the faculty of knowing and for me, impelling and for me, impulse and for me, the plough and for me, rest and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May knowledge be mine, and the power to know; the power to set others to work, and to direct them; the plough, and freedom from what hinders it.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: saṃvid is knowledge of the Veda, the śāstras and the like («वेदशास्त्रादिविज्ञानम्»), and jñātra the capacity to make known («ज्ञापयितृत्वसामर्थ्यम्»). He takes sū and prasū from impelling: «सूः पुत्रादिप्रेरणसामर्थ्यम्», the capacity to direct sons and others, and «प्रसूर्भृत्यादिप्रेरणसामर्थ्यम्», the capacity to direct servants and others. Sīra is the means of farming, the plough and the rest, and laya «तत्प्रतिबन्धनिवृत्तिः», the removal of what hinders it.

flags.note: sū, prasū: Sāyaṇa reads them as powers of directing others (from √sū ‘to impel’); Monier-Williams gives ‘begetting, bringing forth’ (√sū ‘to beget’), as Keith’s ‘begetting, procreation’. laya: Sāyaṇa ‘the removal of what hinders farming’; MW ‘clinging; lying down; rest; dissolution’. The word meanings give the dictionary senses, the contexts Sāyaṇa’s.
The printed bhāṣya’s lemma for jñātra reads शात्रं; the Saṃhitā has ज्ञात्रम्, and his gloss ज्ञापयितृत्व- shows the same word is meant.

samasa.meaning: not dead; as a neuter noun, immortality

samasa.type: nañ-bahuvrīhi, used as a neuter noun
samasa.meaning: free from consumption; as a neuter, health (MW, citing VS)
not causing sickness (MW: an-āmayat, ‘not causing pain’); here, freedom from sickness

samasa.vigraha: दीर्घम् आयुः यस्य सः दीर्घायुः तस्य भावः
samasa.meaning: the state of one whose life is long; long life

samasa.type: nañ-bahuvrīhi, used as a neuter noun
samasa.meaning: having no enemies; as a neuter, freedom from enemies (MW)

vyakarana.note: The text has anāmayac ca, so the stem ends in t: an-āmayat (MW, ‘not causing pain’), apparently a negated present participle of āmayati ‘to be sick’; Sāyaṇa’s lemma is the same (अनामयज्). Used here as a neuter noun beside ayakṣma.
jīvātu, ‘life’ (f., RV, AV) and ‘a life-giving drug’ (MW); Sāyaṇa takes the second sense.

translation.literal: The rite and for me, immortality and for me, freedom from consumption and for me, freedom from sickness and for me, life and for me, long life and for me, freedom from enemies and for me, fearlessness and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May the rite be mine, and its undying fruit; may I be free of grave disease and of lesser sickness; may I have the means of life, and long life; may I be without enemies and without fear.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: ṛta is ritual action, sacrifice and the like («यज्ञादिकर्म»), and amṛta «तत्फलम्», its fruit. Ayakṣma is freedom from grave diseases such as consumption («राजयक्ष्मादिप्रबलव्याधिराहित्यम्»), anāmayat freedom from lesser illnesses such as fever. Jīvātu is «जीवनकारणं व्याधिपरिहारार्थमौषधम्», what keeps one alive: medicine to ward off disease. Dīrghāyutva he explains as freedom from untimely death; anamitra is freedom from foes (वैरिराहित्यम्) and abhaya freedom from fear (भयराहित्यम्).

flags.note: anāmayat: the formation (a negated participle) is inferred from Monier-Williams’ an-āmayat; the sense ‘freedom from sickness’ follows Sāyaṇa and its pairing with ayakṣma.
Sāyaṇa’s gloss on dīrghāyutva is misprinted in the bhāṣya (अपमृत्सुराहित्यम्); its sense, freedom from untimely death, is plain, but it is not quoted.

words.context: Sāyaṇa (here): good going, conduct that all accept (सर्वैरङ्गीकृताचरणम्)
joins each item to the list (Sāyaṇa: समुच्चयार्थः)
with kalpatām, supplied from anuvāka 10: ‘may it be ready for me’
Sāyaṇa: bed, pillow and the like
Sāyaṇa: a fair morning, with bathing, the twilight worship and the rest (स्नानसंध्यावन्दनादियुक्तः शोभनः प्रातःकालः)
Sāyaṇa: a whole day filled with sacrifice, giving, study and the like (यज्ञदानाध्ययनादियुक्तं कृत्स्नं दिनम्)

sandhi.rule: final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23), written as the nasal of the following consonant's class (P. 8.4.59): m + c → ñc

samasa.meaning: good going (the vigraha follows Sāyaṇa’s शोभनगमनं)
a fair dawn (u + u → ū inside the compound); see flags

vyakarana.note: The text reads सूषा च, without visarga, so the word is not the s-stem uṣas (nom. uṣāḥ would give -āś ca) but an ā-stem: su + uṣā ‘dawn’ (MW lists uṣā, f.). Sāyaṇa’s ‘a fair morning’ agrees.
śayana, n. action noun of √śī ‘to lie’: ‘lying down, sleep; a bed’.

translation.literal: Good going and for me, rest and for me, a fair dawn and for me, a fair day and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May my going be good, and my rest; may the dawn be fair for me, and the day.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa glosses this second suga differently from the one in the second anuvāka: «सुगं शोभनगमनं सर्वैरङ्गीकृताचरणमित्यर्थः», good going, that is, conduct that all accept. Śayana is bed, pillow and the like. Sūṣā is «स्नानसंध्यावन्दनादियुक्तः शोभनः प्रातःकालः», a fair morning with bathing, the twilight worship and the rest, and sudina «यज्ञदानाध्ययनादियुक्तं कृत्स्नं दिनम्», the whole day filled with sacrifice, giving and study.
units.reflection: The anuvāka ends on the plainest goods: to go well, to lie down, a fair morning and a fair day. The large goods of the list are lived out in these.

flags.note: sūṣā: Monier-Williams has a sūṣā ‘(prob.) a parturient woman’ (AV) and sūṣas ‘one who enjoys a good dawn’, but not this word in this sense. The analysis su + uṣā ‘fair dawn’ follows Sāyaṇa (शोभनः प्रातःकालः) and Keith (‘fair dawning’), and the sequence with sudina.
